question: How should an ML team plan, research and prepare experimentation so it reaches an MVP quickly without duplicated work or cancelled projects?
contributions: Planning and research workflow for experiments (research, environment, ground rules)
Pre-modelling data analysis for time series (stationarity, decomposition, outliers, ACF/PACF)

limits: Experience-based advice with no measured outcomes; the JFK data analysis is illustrative, not evaluated.
Fig 5.6 ADF numbers and Fig 5.12 readings are images, not in the text layer.
Code uses dated APIs (load_boston, normalize param, statsmodel typo in import, 'seaborn' style) and is explicitly for rapid experimentation only.
The nine-model bake-off itself is deferred to chapter 6; no experiment tracking or model registry tooling is discussed.
practices: Create a clean isolated environment (Docker plus Anaconda, notebook directory mapped to local disk) before experimenting (5.1.1).
Look at the data first, before choosing a model, and write down observations and questions (5.1.1).
Prefer books, papers and API docs over blogs; vet blog ideas by quorum across several independent posts (5.1.1-5.1.2).
Read the API docs of every candidate model's main interface and know which defaults are placeholders (5.1.2).
Keep a library and budget for technical books (5.1.1).
During rapid screening use mostly defaults, mark them or leave a TODO, and do not tune (5.1.2).
Assign each candidate approach to a person or pair and give the phase a deadline (5.1.3).
Fix shared rules: same dataset, metrics, forecast period; visualizations with metrics; code re-runnable from scratch; supportable language and platform (5.1.3).
Pick a primary metric that is comparable across series (MAPE here, because magnitudes differ across airports) but record all applicable metrics (5.1.4).
Do not record categorical metrics for regression or the reverse (sidebar, 5.1.4).
Skip a metric only if its computation cost outweighs its value (5.1.4).
Test stationarity, decompose trend and seasonality, and find outliers before modelling; explain outliers to the business with raw-data plots (5.2.1).
Do not take a seasonal period blindly from the ADF lag count; check it against a decomposition (5.2.1).
Convert scripts to shared functions for ingestion, scoring, visualization and model reports as early as practical, and flag code for it otherwise (5.2.2).
Save generated plots for later reference (5.2.1).
Do not build a package-level project at the experiment stage; that comes in development (5.2.2).
Use string interpolation or f-strings instead of concatenation (sidebar 5.2.2).
Do not overbuild prototypes; speed and objective comparison matter more than accuracy (sidebar 5.1.3).

terms.definition: H0 is that the time series is nonstationary; if the test statistic is less than the critical values, the series is determined as stationary.
A Pearson's test between the time series and lagged values of itself, ranging from -1 to +1; includes direct and indirect effects.
Like autocorrelation but removes the effects previous lag values introduce, measuring the direct lag relationship.
